name: Sam Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the ventilation equipment crew at Iron Gate, a large underground mine. I drive a service vehicle, set heavy fans and duct sections, and test the air before miners go deeper. My two-year technical diploma and years on the job mean I can hear a fan bearing fail before a gauge changes. I like sending crews into safe air, but dragging ducting through wet tunnels is rough on the knees.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are you planning for at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58. My partner Edda and I have grown children and hope I can stop full-time shifts around 64, though we will check the retirement account first. My lead pay is at the high end, we have more than eight months of expenses saved, and several mines nearby use the same equipment. I have never used an AI assistant; I keep the fan readings in my notebook and ask a mechanic when I need advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that fewer forms are welcome, provided somebody still tests the air. I would not put my name on a number copied from a screen. The fans are doing the same job they did yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay and shifts should hold, and our savings give us room if a fan repair closes a tunnel briefly. I do not need a new tool to finish the years I have planned. Edda and I can keep paying into the retirement account as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the fan crew on the current roster and keep recording air readings in my notebook. This month I'd ask the safety manager to keep the manual air test on the shift sheet. In the first year I'd continue the usual retirement account transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The old aches are still there, but work and household money look steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which reading matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the air flow where the duct ends, because a fan can sound strong while a leak steals the air. I write the number down beside the tunnel name. A clean form cannot make a leaking duct safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Edda to use an AI tool for the finances?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner Edda already keeps a clear budget, and we check the account statements together. I would not hand our retirement decision to a chat screen.

say: I would welcome **fewer forms** while keeping manual air tests on every shift.
I would tell the crew the **fan checks** still need a named operator.
think: The **lead wage** and strong reserve make my planned work years feel secure.
I would keep using **paper readings** rather than learn a new AI assistant.
do: Lead the **fan crew** on its usual roster and record tunnel readings.
Ask the **safety manager** to retain manual air tests on shift sheets.
S0.quote: A clean form cannot make a leaking duct safe.
fieldNote: His **manual measurement** is a deliberate safety choice rather than a claim that software never helps.
His **eight-month reserve** and high pay support a steady route toward retirement.

steps.text: Keep leading Iron Gate fan shifts and recording tunnel air readings
Ask safety manager to retain manual air tests on shift sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software can order parts and make schedules, but a duct still has to be fitted in a wet tunnel. If the mine proposes remote fan equipment, I would ask for the trial results. I would not fight a machine that actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My planning duties could be taken over, though the physical job should last longer. A smaller crew might still mean fewer lead hours for me. The savings and other mines give me choices, but losing high pay a few years before stopping would sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current shifts and ask for the mine's written fan equipment plan this quarter. If a remote trial begins, I'd watch the mechanic test a fault before trusting it. In the first year I'd apply to a nearby mine for a lead ventilation post if Iron Gate cuts my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I do not expect an immediate wage loss, but I would watch the next roster closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you a remote fan works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the mechanic to make a fault and show the remote system stopping the fan in time. A sales presentation is not a test. If the record is clean over several shifts, I would accept it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the screen yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn only the controls required to keep my post, on a paid shift with someone beside me. I am slow with new screens, so I would ask for time to practise. I would not volunteer for a course on speculation.

say: I would ask for **trial results** before accepting remote fan equipment.
I would say **parts ordering** changes sooner than fitting ducts underground.
think: My **planning duties** may shrink and eventually take lead hours with them.
Our **savings and nearby mines** offer options if the roster changes.
do: Request a **written fan plan** this quarter and observe any remote fault test.
Apply for a **nearby lead post** if Iron Gate cuts my hours.
feel: **Anxious** about future roster changes, with current pay likely to hold.
S1.quote: A sales presentation is not a test.
fieldNote: He asks for a **fault demonstration** and several shifts of evidence before accepting remote gear.
His **reluctance to study** remains, though he would practise required controls on paid time.

steps.text: Observe a remote fan fault test if Iron Gate runs one
Apply for nearby lead ventilation work if hours fall
Request the written mine fan equipment plan this quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2028 could handle fan orders and shift plans before robots can fit ducting. The card puts capable hands-on robots around 2031. I would want the mine to give each worker the dates and terms in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when planning changes and 63 around the robot date, one year before I hoped to stop. The mine could cut the lead post early and then replace much of the physical work. Edda and I have enough savings to avoid panic, but I would need to count any lost wage against retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the retirement office for written estimates at 63 and 64 this month. I'd pause our planned boat purchase and put the monthly amount into cash savings. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for a manual ventilation lead post at another mine if one is open, rather than pay for an unproven course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The savings give me a plan, but a lost year of good pay would change what Edda and I can afford later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an early package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after Edda and I compare an actual offer with the retirement estimates. I would not leave a good wage because someone says robots are coming. If the package covers the gap, we could consider it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the cash account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money we had set aside for boat payments would go into a separate account each month. We can still borrow a boat for a weekend. I would rather have the cash if the roster thins.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning** from the 2031 hands-on robot risk.
I would ask for **written terms** before deciding whether to leave the mine.
think: A **lead wage cut** could arrive before I reach 64, with physical work threatened later.
Our **strong reserve** prevents panic, yet lost pay could reduce retirement choices.
do: Delay the **boat purchase** and transfer its planned payment into cash savings.
Get **retirement estimates** and apply for an open manual lead post after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about a lost year of high pay, with a financial plan.
S2.quote: I would not leave a good wage because someone says robots are coming.
fieldNote: He uses **written retirement estimates** rather than assuming a package would cover the gap.
The **boat delay** adds cash without claiming that saved spending alone replaces wages.

steps.text: Delay buying the planned family boat this year
Transfer the planned boat payment into cash savings monthly
Apply for an open nearby manual ventilation lead post after 2028
Request pension estimates at 63 and 64 before choosing retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 could take the fan schedules when I am 63, while capable hands-on robots come around 2034. That gives the mine time to publish a sensible staffing plan. I would want the physical crews protected through an actual trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our retirement account is enough, I could stop full-time work at 64 before the robot date. The risk is my lead planning duties being cut at 63, one year before then. I might find a similar post nearby, but I would rather finish at Iron Gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the fan roster and get a written retirement estimate this year. I'd add one hundred a month to our retirement account while the pay holds. In the first year after 2031, if my lead hours fall, I'd take a regular fan operator shift only if the pay still covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The long gap to robots helps, but a shortfall in my final working year would still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why accept a regular operator shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the fans, and one year of reliable pay could protect the retirement account. I would check the monthly offer with Edda first. A lower title would not bother me; an unpaid bill would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on the remote fan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sit through paid training if the mine needed it for a real operator post. I would not spend our money on a certificate just to appear interested. I still prefer the equipment I can hear.

say: I would ask for a **staffing plan** before 2031 planning changes reach my lead post.
I would remind the crew **2034 robots** follow three years after thinking AI.
think: I could **stop at 64** before physical robots arrive if the retirement account supports it.
A **one-year lead cut** could still weaken our final savings.
do: Add **one hundred monthly** to retirement savings while the lead wage holds.
Take a **regular fan shift** after 2031 if offered at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about one final year of pay, with a plausible bridge.
S3.quote: A lower title would not bother me; an unpaid bill would.
fieldNote: His **title flexibility** contrasts with his reluctance to learn a new screen.
He would train only for a **real paid post**, not a speculative certificate.

steps.text: Add one hundred monthly to the retirement account while pay holds
Take a regular fan operator shift if offered at bill-covering pay
Request written retirement income at 64 before choosing a stopping date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a decade is enough time to test equipment properly. AGI by 2036 may take planning work, and capable hands-on robots arrive around 2039. I would still ask for a named worker responsible for air tests until the last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036 and 71 at the robot date. If Edda and I can afford the planned stop at 64, my own mine wage is finished before either change. I would worry more about younger ventilation workers who still need decades of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current shifts this year and ask for a retirement account estimate at 64. I'd continue the scheduled contributions and review the figure with Edda every year. In the first year after 2036, if I have retired, I would help younger crews check old tunnel plans when they ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own job and income if the retirement figures work. I would still want the mine to treat current workers fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change the retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the written retirement estimate cannot cover our bills, I would work longer while my knees allow. The robot dates are later, so I have time to adjust. I would make that decision from the account statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them to keep their safety records and demand paid practice on new fans. The younger ventilation workers' wages matter after I am gone. I can help them read the old tunnel plans, but I cannot choose their careers.

say: I would ask for **tested equipment** and a named worker responsible for air checks.
I would tell younger crews the **2036 and 2039** dates leave time for paid practice.
think: My **planned stop at 64** falls before either technology date if retirement income covers bills.
Younger workers still face **longer income risk** from the eventual equipment change.
do: Keep **fan shifts** this year and obtain a written retirement estimate at 64.
Review **account statements** with Edda annually before deciding when to stop.
feel: **Calm** about my own wage if retirement income is adequate.
S4.quote: The younger ventilation workers' wages matter after I am gone.
fieldNote: His **own income** is likely secure on this timeline, subject to the retirement account.
He stays engaged with **safety records** for younger staff while avoiding technology courses himself.

steps.text: Keep leading Iron Gate ventilation shifts this year
Review written retirement estimates with Edda before choosing a stopping date

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Planning could change at 60 and physical fan work around 63, before I hope to stop at 64. A written staffing schedule, a fair package if my post goes, and a paid manual role nearby would help me choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens to the air when the power goes out. I know which fan to restart first because I have walked those tunnels. A plan should name the person who will know which fan to restart first after I leave.

headlineQuote: A plan should name the person who will know which fan to restart first after I leave.
portrait: **Sam Ziegler**, 58, leads ventilation equipment work at a large underground mine and knows the fans by sound.
His **high pay**, strong savings and many nearby mines give him choices as he and his partner approach retirement.
He **never uses AI**, prefers his notebook and would learn new controls only for a real paid role.
The **fastest AGI** path threatens a final year of wages; longer paths may let him finish before physical robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut lead duties at 60 and physical fan work around 63, ahead of his hoped-for stop.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing schedule**, fair package if displaced and an available paid manual role nearby would help.
